verses.text: When all the kings of the Amorites, who were beyond the Jordan westward, and all the kings of the Canaanites, who were by the sea, heard how Yahweh had dried up the waters of the Jordan from before the children of Israel, until we had crossed over, their heart melted, and there was no more spirit in them, because of the children of Israel.
At that time, Yahweh said to Joshua, “Make flint knives, and circumcise again the sons of Israel the second time.”
Joshua made himself flint knives, and circumcised the sons of Israel at the hill of the foreskins.
This is the reason Joshua circumcised them: all the people who came out of Egypt, who were males, even all the men of war, died in the wilderness along the way, after they came out of Egypt.
For all the people who came out were circumcised; but all the people who were born in the wilderness along the way as they came out of Egypt had not been circumcised.

For the children of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, even the men of war who came out of Egypt, were consumed, because they didn’t listen to Yahweh’s voice. Yahweh swore to them that he wouldn’t let them see the land which Yahweh swore to their fathers that he would give us, a land flowing with milk and honey.
Their children, whom he raised up in their place, were circumcised by Joshua; for they were uncircumcised, because they had not circumcised them on the way.
When they were done circumcising the whole nation, they stayed in their places in the camp until they were healed.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt off of you.” Therefore the name of that place was called Gilgal,  to this day.
The children of Israel encamped in Gilgal. They kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month at evening in the plains of Jericho.
They ate unleavened cakes and parched grain of the produce of the land on the next day after the Passover, in the same day.
The manna ceased on the next day, after they had eaten of the produce of the land. The children of Israel didn’t have manna any more; but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.

When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man stood in front of him with his sword drawn in his hand. Joshua went to him and said to him, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?”
He said, “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.” Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and worshiped, and asked him, “What does my lord say to his servant?”
The prince of Yahweh’s army said to Joshua, “Take your shoes off of your feet; for the place on which you stand is holy.” Joshua did so.

footnotes.content: Word travels fast—the news of what Yahweh did at the Jordan reached the kings before Israel even arrived. When enemies hear what the Lord has done, fear arrives before the sword. Their hearts melted because they'd seen Him at work, not because they doubted His power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Flint knives: the tools of covenant, sharp and true. Yahweh speaks and asks Joshua to circumcise the whole nation again—not because the old sign was erased, but because a new generation must carry it forward. This is how the Lord marks His people in each age.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua obeyed without hesitation. He took the flint knife and did the work. The place got its name—the Hill of Foreskins—a stark monument to the moment when a new generation entered the covenant. No shame in obedience; the shame lay in the forty years behind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the sober accounting: all the men of war who left Egypt never reached Canaan. They died in the wilderness, worn down by their own refusal to trust. The old generation's disobedience had a cost that time alone could not erase—though mercy came to their children.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ones born along the way—in tents and dust and uncertainty—had not been marked with the sign. Now that we stand at the threshold, Yahweh calls us to complete what the wilderness could not. The covenant belongs to those who enter the land, not just those who escaped Egypt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty years. One generation's refusal—they would not believe His promise—meant their children grew up in exile from a land they'd never seen. Yet Yahweh kept them alive in the wilderness, held them, brought them through. He didn't break His oath, even when they broke their faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The children stepped into their place. Joshua circumcised them—all those born in the wilderness—and gave them the sign their parents had neglected. A second generation gets to carry forward what the first refused. Mercy often works this way: not erasing the past, but reopening the door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Healing takes time. The whole nation lay in camp, recovering, vulnerable. Yet Yahweh asked them to be still, to rest in His care at the edge of the promised land. Sometimes the Lord makes us pause before He moves, so we know it is His strength, not ours, that takes the city.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt off of you." Gilgal—the name means the rolling away. What a comfort: the shame and wandering don't follow us forever. When we step into covenant with Yahweh, He removes the old weight. Gilgal stands as a marker of that mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here at Gilgal, the children of Israel kept the Passover—the same feast their parents had eaten the night they left Egypt. Now they eat it again at the threshold of the land. The rhythm of worship continues; the covenant meal connects the beginning and the promise that draws near.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the Passover came the produce of the land—unleavened cakes and parched grain from Canaan itself. For the first time, the new generation ate from a harvest sown by no one they knew. The land Yahweh promised was feeding them. Faith became sight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The manna stopped. For forty years it fell each morning, a daily sign of the Lord's care in the wasteland. Now that we taste the land's fruit, we don't need it anymore. The wilderness season ends; the settled season begins. Yahweh's faithfulness changes form, but never fails.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua stood near Jericho and saw a man with a sword drawn—a warrior ready for battle. He asked the sharp question: are you with us or against us? Every help we see must be weighed. Joshua didn't assume; he inquired. Wisdom meets the stranger with respect and a clear mind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am commander of Yahweh's army." Joshua fell to his face and worshiped. The battle belongs to the Lord; our part is to serve as His instrument, not to boast of our strength. Joshua learned in that instant that Jericho's walls would fall because the commander of heaven had already taken His stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Take your shoes off; the place is holy." Just as Moses met the Lord at the burning bush, Joshua stood on sacred ground—not a temple, but the presence of Yahweh's commander. We enter the greatest battles barefoot, knowing we stand where the Holy One dwells.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
